Oct 27, 2026

## **Fast Finality \+ Networking**

Invited [Sukun Tarachandani](mailto:sukun.tarachandani@ethereum.org) [raul.kripalani@ethereum.org](mailto:raul.kripalani@ethereum.org) [Ben Edgington](mailto:ben.edgington@ethereum.org) [Roberto Saltini](mailto:roberto.saltini@ethereum.org) [Yann Vonlanthen](mailto:yann.vonlanthen@ethereum.org) [Kamil Salakhiev](mailto:kamil.salakhiev@ethereum.org) [francesco@ethlabs.org](mailto:francesco@ethlabs.org) [anton.nashatyrev@consensys.com](mailto:anton.nashatyrev@consensys.com) [mikhail.kalinin@consensys.com](mailto:mikhail.kalinin@consensys.com) [barnabe@ethlabs.org](mailto:barnabe@ethlabs.org) [Csaba Kiraly](mailto:csaba.kiraly@ethereum.org) [Kevaundray Wedderburn](mailto:kevaundray.wedderburn@ethereum.org) [pablo.deymonnaz@lambdaclass.com](mailto:pablo.deymonnaz@lambdaclass.com) [mega@lambdaclass.com](mailto:mega@lambdaclass.com) [francesco.damato@ethlabs.org](mailto:francesco.damato@ethlabs.org)

Attachments [Fast Finality + Networking](https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?eid=M2xrYm12c2Y2cThqbXBodW5pc200ZzF1bXNfMjAyNjExMDNUMTIwMDAwWiBzdWt1bi50YXJhY2hhbmRhbmlAZXRoZXJldW0ub3Jn)

Meeting records [Transcript](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1q7ilPFVyZ1LTnfLx99C41_URm0SGy9MeUzQiiTzQLxw/edit?usp=drive_web&tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu) 

### **Summary**

Prioritization prototypes and simulation models evaluated network congestion and validator round structures.

**Prioritization and Bandwidth Testing**  
Prototyping revealed performance drops during peer congestion. Consensus favored continuing a minimal specification for decoupled consensus.

**Validator Simulation Models**  
Simulations analyzed tree shapes and 1 million validator distributions. Aggregation costs were calculated at 45000 dollars annually.

**Network Topologies and Trees**  
Evaluated 8-to-1 aggregation tree configurations for faster proof delivery. Super nodes held 96 percent of stake.

### **Decisions**

## Needs Further Discussion

* **Committee approach as provisional default structure** The team deliberated using committees as the provisional default approach while investigating potential removal, leaving the final architecture open for further discussion.

## Aligned

* **Minimal specification approach for decoupled consensus** The group aligned on proceeding with a minimal specification for decoupled consensus using standard networking features while keeping prioritization research independent for potential future integration.

### **Next steps**

- [ ] \[Sukun\] Discuss Prioritization: Present the prioritization and Peer-to-Peer concerns at the upcoming networking meeting.

- [ ] \[The group\] Build Devnet Simulation: Construct a devnet simulation with worst-case bandwidth scenarios to evaluate whether Goldfish votes are delivered within the assumed time bounds.

- [ ] \[Kamil Salakhiev\] Fix Duplicate Issues: Refine the simulation code to resolve the long tail of duplicate message arrivals. Disable unnecessary flags to ensure cleaner message propagation.

- [ ] \[Kamil Salakhiev\] Design Propagation: Develop a structured approach for aggregation propagation that minimizes bandwidth overhead. Design the mechanism to maintain censorship resistance while preventing store and forward delays.

- [ ] \[Kevaundray Wedderburn\] Document Research: Compile notes and answers to outstanding questions regarding network propagation and committee structures. Document these findings to resolve current uncertainties.

- [ ] \[The group\] Discuss Pipelining: Conduct further deliberations on the pipelining question asynchronously. Coordinate the discussion via the internal communication channels.

### **Details**

**Prioritization Prototype and Simulation**: Anton Nashatyrev presented a web-coded prototype for prioritization relying on quick streams, noting that while simulation results are positive between two peers, performance drops when multiple peers are involved due to inbound congestion and lack of visibility into other peers' congestion states ([00:00:05](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.dxphktwwnasc)). Anton Nashatyrev explained that inbound congestion causes peers to send unimportant data because they do not know what is happening with the receiver's congestion, and while choking can help, it introduces latency ([00:06:12](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.t3uxgyzd1s8)).

---

**Alternative Perspectives on Prioritization and Bandwidth**: Csaba Kiraly shared that their own experiments indicate inbound bandwidth is rarely the bottleneck on current mainnet nodes, noting that prioritization machinery is hard to measure and that lower-hanging fruits like avoiding sending late data exist ([00:07:45](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.udtr1wlcqbyq)). Csaba Kiraly stated that to force congestion to a level where prioritization matters, bandwidth had to be reduced to 5 megabits per second, and questioned whether prioritization actually solves the specific problems intended ([00:09:15](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.v8wdqfl7efz1)).

---

**Decoupled Consensus and Goldfish Message Delivery Risks**: Kevaundray Wedderburn raised the question of whether prioritization is necessary for decoupled consensus and if experiments can determine this. Roberto Saltini expressed concern that without prioritization, goldfish messages might be delayed beyond assumed delivery times, making the goldfish chain unsafe, while Sukun Tarachandani argued that staggering publishes already ensures goldfish messages are delivered on time based on their measurements ([00:11:54](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.u68jv2j8wvov)).

---

**Evaluating Staggering Versus Network-Level Prioritization**: Csaba Kiraly discussed whether staggering successfully avoids trouble by delaying traffic, but noted it gives up headroom and doesn't handle outages as effectively as a non-staggered system could under worst-case assumptions ([00:14:57](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.mjemdd7ap9n4)) ([00:19:12](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.bacri0xnyy6x)). Sukun Tarachandani responded that staggering works well within eight-slot rounds because the network has enough aggregate bandwidth to support them, noting that P99 metrics showed goldfish votes were received within a second even with 25% higher load ([00:20:28](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.tsmh7fo6dyj6)).

---

**Integrating Priority Systems Into Design Specifications**: Sukun Tarachandani suggested starting with current proposals that work now and adding traffic priority systems later as they get client-feature-integrated. Csaba Kiraly noted that the features being discussed are not currently client-feature-integrated window items and that building complex combinations presents design challenges, though they remained open to exploring prioritization if it offers a clear research edge ([00:21:32](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.q9xliya0cuyg)) ([00:24:31](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.8za95h5uhn9a)).

---

**Minimal Specification Consensus and Bandwidth Limitation Testing**: Yann Vonlanthen summarized the consensus to continue working on a minimal specification for decoupled consensus using edge-start items on networking, with independent research continuing on prioritization. Roberto Saltini proposed creating an artificial "devil network" where bandwidth is always at the worst-case scenario peak to test if goldfish votes are delivered on time, while Csaba Kiraly noted Ethereum testnets historically ran with near-infinite bandwidth without bandwidth-limited testing ([00:27:01](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.6v86j18ykc7x)). Yann Vonlanthen asked about topic-specific bandwidth limits, and Csaba Kiraly explained that application-layer machinery like token buckets can enforce traffic class guarantees ([00:28:21](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.fs9iofiokell)).

---

**Bandwidth Allocation and Client Team Implementation Challenges**: Ben Edgington emphasized that bandwidth must be allocated to time-bound head and goldfish votes first, with FFG votes fitting around them rather than receiving guaranteed bandwidth ([00:29:43](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.bxmke97g5g7v)). Sukun Tarachandani and Csaba Kiraly discussed client team implementation challenges, noting that client teams generally work on scheduled fork requirements and often require mainnet proof before implementing optional features, which is difficult to demonstrate for future adverse conditions ([00:32:23](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.1vi5i6k5rx13)).

---

**Transitioning to Post-Quantum and Committee Round Structure Discussions**: Roberto Saltini suggested that prioritization could be important for post-quantum requirements by allowing FFG attestation scheduling to be independent of slot time ([00:33:36](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.rqavw51dhbhd)). Yann Vonlanthen then transitioned the meeting to discuss round structures and post-quantum considerations, prompting Barnabé Monnot to present their model and simulations ([00:36:37](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.wekweagz1v1k)).

---

**Barnabé Monnot's Validator and Network Simulation Model**: Barnabé Monnot presented a high-level model starting with validator set distributions, hardware requirements (such as blob custody and subnet subscriptions), and adversarial percentages set to a 5% fault tolerance ([00:37:52](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.7qx4ukgpygd9)). Barnabé Monnot reported that the simulation derived an optimal tree shape of 1,024 groups for one million validators, with a total network aggregation cost of approximately \$45,000 per year (about 0.027% of rewards), indicating that validator incentives for aggregation may not be strictly necessary ([00:40:52](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.qfrluf14vjp7)).

---

**Thread Counts, Subrounds, and Validator Committee Assignments**: Kevaundray Wedderburn asked about thread configurations, to which Barnabé Monnot clarified that basic nodes were assumed to have 16 threads using 50% for aggregation (8 threads) ([00:45:56](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.af7i3q335ohv)). Kamil Salakhiev and Kevaundray Wedderburn discussed whether all one million validators vote simultaneously or across subrounds, with Kamil Salakhiev suggesting an optimization for 131k validators per subround to reduce bandwidth and aggregate fewer signatures at once ([00:47:36](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.odllqeepvit)).

---

**Subrounds, Proposal Reward Variance, and One-Shot Burst Debates**: Kevaundray Wedderburn noted that subrounds help reduce proposal reward variance by preventing proposers from missing aggregations over an eight-slot round, though it complicates post-quantum designs. Barnabé Monnot and Yann Vonlanthen debated whether a one-shot burst or committee load balancing is better for the network, with Barnabé Monnot supporting one-shot bursts assuming the network throttles and handles congestion itself, while Yann Vonlanthen expressed worry about skewed rewards for large entities like Binance or Lido ([00:51:24](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.g0jmbgyzasz7)). Kevaundray Wedderburn, Barnabé Monnot, and Kamil Salakhiev discussed late votes, stake consolidation (such as Coinbase holding 8%), and whether uplink queues can handle one-shot bursts from large entities hosting thousands of validators ([00:55:23](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.2cf66vdo5i5d)) ([00:57:49](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.vxfo6sosf138)).

---

**Validator Load and Blind Queuing Concerns**: Kamil Salakhiev raised concerns regarding massive peers hosting up to 3,000 validators that generate thousands of signatures and must download and upload them if they end up on the same subnet ([00:59:24](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.h7mejo8hisxw)). Csaba Kiraly explained that blind queuing leads to network inefficiencies by removing opportunities to eliminate duplicate work before scheduling ([01:00:35](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.202dffnve4ez)).

---

**Network Congestion and Congestion Collapse Debates**: Sukun Tarachandani argued that congestion collapse is largely mitigated today by fair queuing mechanisms implemented by internet service providers and routers, making it reliable to publish messages at the start of a slot ([01:01:47](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.8b6xd1peeh85)). Conversely, Csaba Kiraly and Barnabé Monnot expressed concerns about potential congestion collapse and nonlinear slowdowns when flooding the network with data simultaneously, with Csaba citing historical issues where handling in-forking workloads caused client degradation ([01:03:01](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.yn9u7up0ts5i)). Sukun suggested that simultaneous publishing could be faster in aggregate despite losing uniform throughput ([01:05:27](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.lictzjyde5o)).

---

**Committee Versus Oneshot Network Approaches**: Kevaundray Wedderburn proposed using committees as the default approach since it mirrors current systems, despite acknowledging potential inefficiencies ([01:05:27](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.lictzjyde5o)). Yann Vonlanthen and Kevaundray discussed the benefits of a oneshot, committee-free approach, noting that it provides greater flexibility, enables large validators to aggregate locally, and permits optimistic lower-duplication strategies, though the committee approach remains the more de-risked baseline ([01:06:57](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.scw6xdl40kob)).

---

**Simulation of the Committee Approach and Network Topologies**: Kamil Salakhiev shared simulation results generated using Shadow based on a decoupled consensus model featuring 1 million validators split across eight sub-rounds of 131,000 voting validators distributed among 30,000 peer hosts. The simulation modeled a naive gossip sub and an aggregator tree structure, assuming a network composition of 80 percent home nodes with 100 megabits down link and 50 megabits up link bandwidth, and 20 percent super nodes hosting more than 10 validators with 1 gigabit symmetric bandwidth, which accounted for 96 percent of the stake ([01:09:43](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.2aty5kn5sjxk)) ([01:13:48](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.aw6d2r72v6tj)).

---

**Propagation Mechanisms and Network Resilience**: Kamil Salakhiev described an announcement pool mechanism where aggregators advertise proofs once they collect 90 percent of signatures ([01:16:04](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.dpo6m1ri9kfo)). Kevaundray Wedderburn questioned whether a 3 to 4-second window is sufficient for vote propagation and raised concerns about network degradation if super nodes fail. Kamil noted that because super nodes hold 96 percent of the stake, their failure would cause the network to go down, though Kamil viewed the aggregation tree primarily as a fallback mechanism while expecting sophisticated entities to subscribe to all subnets independently ([01:18:30](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.5qaaxsq6drft)) ([01:20:57](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.9v5w8gfzhxpc)).

---

**Comparison of Two-to-One and Eight-to-One Aggregation Trees**: Kamil Salakhiev compared two-to-one and eight-to-one aggregation tree configurations, reporting that the eight-to-one structure achieved the final proof slightly faster at 5.43 seconds compared to 6.12 seconds for the two-to-one structure, while significantly reducing network complexity. Consequently, Kamil expressed a preference for the eight-to-one approach if EIP-787 requirements permit ([01:23:22](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.yfkfga1bsiad)).

---

**Final Proof Distribution and Post-Quantum Proof Determinism**: Kamil Salakhiev and Kevaundray Wedderburn discussed the distribution of final proofs from aggregators to proposers, noting that multiple final proofs require a K-to-many propagation design rather than a one-to-many approach ([01:26:02](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.ovxyw3ce25i4)). Furthermore, Kevaundray highlighted that in Post-Quantum cryptography, proofs are non-deterministic due to internal proof-of-work mechanisms, meaning identical bitlists do not guarantee identical proofs and preventing the use of standard content identifiers ([01:27:20](?tab=t.eorgvcs3l1iu#heading=h.qbk75midlpqj)).
